title: Double Status Credit Offers Used to Mean Something
body:
Australian Frequent Flyer
Australian Frequent Flyer - Tips, Tricks and Chat for Australian Frequent Flyers
Virgin Australia and Qantas Boeing 737s. Photo: Jonathan Wong.
Remember when a double status credit offer from Qantas or Virgin Australia was actually something to get excited about?
In October 2026, both airlines launched yet another round of bonus status credit promotions. Velocity offered double status credits or points, while Qantas Business Rewards ran its own double status credit promotion.
These offers are normally fantastic news for frequent flyers looking to earn or retain status. But with promotions now appearing almost every month, I can’t help but wonder whether Qantas and Virgin Australia are killing the very thing that made them so effective.
When double status credits were worth waiting for
In the years immediately following COVID-19, one of the most common questions on the AFF forum I saw was when the next double status credit (DSC) offer would arrive.
It became such a frequent question that members even had a templated response ready to go! Or, some now choose to play bingo with inevitable follow ups…
Courtesy of @DejaBrew on the AFF forum.
Back then, things were quite different. Both Qantas and Virgin Australia were enjoying full planes and high airfares, while large numbers of frequent flyers continued to hold status thanks to COVID-era extensions.
With plenty of elite members already filling airport lounges, and little need to incentivise forward bookings, neither airline had much reason to offer additional status credits. Status was achievable enough already – part of Velocity’s justification for its 2024 status program changes was that status had become too easy to earn.
When an offer finally landed, it felt like a frenzy. Frequent flyers would rush to book months’ worth of travel during the week-long booking window, often specifically holding off on making reservations until the next promotion. Even Australian public servants were getting in on the action .
But somewhere along the line, the strategy changed.
Eleven bonus status credit promotions in 2026 (so far)
By my count, Velocity has launched six publicly available double or bonus status credit promotions so far in 2026:
Bonus status credits between January and March
Virgin Australia Holidays double status credits in March
Double points or status credits in May
Another double status credit offer in June
Double status credits with Virgin Australia Holidays in July
The latest October promotion
Qantas isn’t far behind, with five promotions of its own:
February’s double status credits
Another promotion in May
Double status credits in September
October’s Qantas Business Rewards promotion
Double status credits to Paris in November
Of course, not all these promotions are identical. Some target particular types of bookings, while others have different travel windows.
This number of status credit promotions hasn’t come out of the blue. Plenty of lucrative offers were available in previous years, such as a (ridiculous) triple status credits offer with Velocity in 2025 .
But the broader trend is unmistakable. There is now a bonus status credit promotion from one airline or the other almost every month.
Are Airlines Killing Their Own Promotions?
Obviously, I can understand why airlines run double status credit promotions. They’re an effective way to incentivise bookings, bring forward revenue and encourage frequent flyers to spend more.
But I think the increasingly frequent promotions risk undermining their own effectiveness.
Part of the appeal of double status credits was always their scarcity. If you knew an offer might not come around for another year, there was a genuine incentive to book as much future travel as possible during that single week. Now, what’s the rush?
If Qantas or Velocity launches another promotion every couple of months, why bother planning your entire year’s travel around one booking window? You can simply assume another offer will be around the corner.
Suddenly, the urgency disappears. Frequent flyers can make more rational booking decisions rather than frantically booking everything during one promotion.
The recent Qantas Business Rewards offer even coincided with a New Zealand airfare sale, particularly interesting given the popularity of New Zealand status runs .
Queenstown, New Zealand. Photo: Qantas.
Of course, airlines still win when frequent flyers book additional flights purely to earn status credits. But the effectiveness of these promotions as a way to generate incremental bookings must surely diminish when they become so predictable.
Short-Term Revenue, Long-Term Damage
Velocity’s recent offers are particularly interesting. Some have featured incredibly short travel windows, making them useless for anyone planning travel further ahead.
To me, these feel increasingly like short-term attempts to boost forward bookings, rather than carefully considered loyalty promotions. Some, with especially restricted booking windows, appear like somebody trying to meet a middle-management revenue target – by pressing the ‘magic DSC button’. Perhaps that’s unfair, but many of these offers are clearly not meant for the wider travelling public.
And there’s another problem. If the next promotion is likely to be just as restrictive as the last, frequent flyers might simply stop paying attention. It just feels that both airlines are sacrificing the long-term effectiveness of one of their best promotions for a short-term revenue boost.
Do you think bonus status credit offers have become too common? Share your thoughts on the AFF forum.
